sketches: In a 2-colouring of K_{2n-2}, some colour class has at least (n-1)(2n-3)/2 > (n-1)(n-2) = N(k-1)/2 edges with N=2n-2, k=n-1. Erdős–Sós then gives every tree with n-1 edges (n vertices) in that colour, so r(T,T) <= 2n-2.

source.name: Erdős–Sós conjecture
source.statement: If $G$ is a simple graph on $n$ vertices with $m > n(k-1)/2$ edges, then $G$ contains every tree with $k$ edges.

sketches: If G has no K_{t+1} minor, Hadwiger gives chi(G) <= t, so some colour class is an independent set of size >= n/t. The arXiv node's own context calls this the standard weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture.

source.name: Hadwiger's conjecture
source.context: Known for $k \le 6$: the case $k = 5$ is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem (Wagner 1937) and $k = 6$ was settled by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (1993).

target.name: Independence number lower bound in K_{t+1}-minor-free graphs
target.statement: For every positive integer $t$, if an $n$-vertex graph $G$ does not contain $K_{t+1}$ as a minor then $\alpha(G) \geq n/t$.
target.context: This conjecture is a natural weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture: since Hadwiger's conjecture would imply every $n$-vertex $K_{t+1}$-minor-free graph has chromatic number at most $t$ and thus an independent set of size at least $n/t$, this bound has attracted considerable attention (see Seymour's survey [31]). Duchet and Meyniel proved the bound holds within a factor of 2 in 1982, and subsequent improvements have been made by Fox, Balogh–Kostochka, and others. The present paper studies this conjecture restricted to triangle-free graphs.

sketches: Albertson's conjecture (chi>=t implies cr(G)>=cr(K_t)) weakens Hajós: a K_t-subdivision has crossing number >= cr(K_t). So Hajós for k=5,6 implies Albertson's conjecture for t=5,6. Only those instances follow, not the general statement, and those instances are already known.

source.name: Hajós conjecture for $k = 5$ and $k = 6$
source.statement: Does every $k$-chromatic graph contain a subdivision of $K_k$ when $k = 5$ and when $k = 6$?
source.context: Hajós conjectured this for all $k$; it holds for $k \le 4$ (Dirac 1952) and Catlin (1979) disproved it for every $k \ge 7$.

target.name: Crossing numbers and coloring
target.statement: We let $ cr(G) $ denote the crossing number of a graph $ G $ . Conjecture Every graph $ G $ with $ \chi(G) \ge t $ satisfies $ cr(G) \ge cr(K_t) $ .
target.context: This conjecture is an interesting weakening of the disproved Hajos Conjecture which asserted that $ \chi(G) \ge t $ implies that $ G $ contains a subdivision of $ K_t $ . A minimal counterexample to Albertson's conjecture is critical, with minimum degree $ \ge t $ . Using this and the crossing lemma, Albertson, Cranston and Fox showed that a minimum counterexample has at most $ 4t $ vertices. They then analyzed small cases to show that the conjecture holds for $ t \le 12 $ . More recently, Barat and Toth [BT] sharpened these arguments to show that the conjecture holds for $ t \le 16 $ .

sketches: A K_k-subdivision is a K_k-minor, so Hajós for k implies Hadwiger for the same k. Here only the cases k=5,6 are involved, which are already known for Hadwiger (Wagner+4CT, Robertson–Seymour–Thomas), so the general Hadwiger node is not implied.

source.name: Hajós conjecture for $k = 5$ and $k = 6$
source.statement: Does every $k$-chromatic graph contain a subdivision of $K_k$ when $k = 5$ and when $k = 6$?
source.context: Hajós conjectured this for all $k$; it holds for $k \le 4$ (Dirac 1952) and Catlin (1979) disproved it for every $k \ge 7$.

target.name: Hadwiger's conjecture
target.context: Known for $k \le 6$: the case $k = 5$ is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem (Wagner 1937) and $k = 6$ was settled by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (1993).

sketches: The hypergraph conjecture c(H)=O(sqrt(n/k)) for connected k-uniform hypergraphs specializes at k=2 to c(G)=O(sqrt(n)) for connected graphs, which is Meyniel's conjecture (cops-and-robbers on a 2-graph is the usual game). The paper itself notes it implies Meyniel even for k=n^alpha, alpha<1.

source.name: Cop number √(n/k) bound for k-uniform hypergraphs
source.statement: Let $H$ be a connected $k$-graph on $n$ vertices. Then $c(H) = O\!\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{n}{k}}\right)$.
source.context: The authors introduce this as a generalisation of Meyniel's conjecture to $k$-uniform hypergraphs, motivated by a blow-up construction that shows $c(H) = \Omega\!\left(\sqrt{n/k}\right)$ is achievable. They further observe that for any polynomial $k = n^\alpha$ with $\alpha < 1$, Conjecture 1.4 implies Meyniel's conjecture.

target.name: Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number
target.statement: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices has cop number $c(G) \le C\sqrt{n}$.
target.context: In the game of Cops and Robbers, $k$ cops choose vertices, then the robber chooses a vertex, and the two sides alternate moves (cops first), each piece moving to a vertex at distance at most one; the cops win if a cop occupies the robber's vertex. The cop number $c(G)$ is the least $k$ for which the cops have a winning strategy. Writing $c(n)$ for the maximum of $c(G)$ over connected graphs of order $n$, the conjecture says $c(n) = O(\sqrt{n})$; it is equivalent to $M_k = \Omega(k^2)$, where $M_k$ is the minimum order of a connected graph with cop number $k$ (Baird et al. 2014). The bound would be tight up to the constant: incidence graphs of projective planes give $c(n) \ge \sqrt{n/2} - o(\sqrt n)$.

sketches: Fleischner and Jackson (1989) showed Thomassen's line-graph conjecture (equivalent to Matthews-Sumner by Ryjacek's closure) is equivalent to: every cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph has a dominating cycle C (every edge meets C). In a cubic graph, vertices off such C form an independent set each with 3 neighbours on C, while each vertex of C has at most one neighbour off C, so |C| >= 3(n-|C|), i.e. |C| >= 3n/4, giving Bondy's linear-cycle conjecture with c=3/4.

source.name: Matthews–Sumner conjecture
source.context: Equivalent, via Ryjáček's closure, to Thomassen's conjecture that every 4-connected line graph is Hamiltonian.

target.name: Bondy's linear-length cycle conjecture for cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs
target.statement: There is a positive constant $c$ such that every 3-connected, cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph on $n$ vertices contains a cycle of length at least $cn$.
target.context: Attributed to J.A. Bondy; see Fleischner and Jackson (1989).

sketches: For a 3-connected cubic planar graph G, the prism G x K_2 is the graph of a simple 4-polytope (prism over a simple 3-polytope), so Barnette's 4-polytope conjecture restricted to prisms says G x K_2 is Hamiltonian, which is also a consequence of the Hamilton-decomposition conjecture for such prisms. Neither statement implies the other in general.

source.name: Barnette's conjecture on 4-regular 4-polytopes
source.statement: The graph of every 4-regular 4-polytope (every simple 4-dimensional convex polytope) is Hamiltonian.
source.context: Attributed to D.W. Barnette; see Grünbaum (1970), p. 1145.

target.name: Hamilton decomposition of prisms over 3-connected cubic planar graphs
target.statement: Conjecture Every prism over a $ 3 $ -connected cubic planar graph can be decomposed into two Hamilton cycles.
target.context: The prism over a graph $ G $ is the Cartesian product $ G\square K_2 $ . Rosenfeld and Barnette [RB] deduced from the Four-Colour Theorem that the prism over cubic planar 3-connected $ G $ has a Hamilton cycle $ C $ . The graph $ G\setminus E(C) $ is cycle factor (spanning union of cycles). The conjecture says that one can choses $ C $ so that the cycle factor $ G\setminus E(C) $ has a unique cycle, that is a Hamilton cycle.
